analysis.one_liner: Simplifies income tax to three rates applied to all income, expands family credits, and sets a flat 35% corporate tax.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors in April 2006, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the individual income tax around three rates (15%, 25%, 35%) applied to every kind of income, including capital gains and dividends, which currently enjoy lower rates. It would roughly double the standard deduction, replace the earned income and child credits with a simpler $2,500-per-child family credit, create a refundable college credit of up to $3,000, let non-itemizers deduct mortgage interest, replace IRAs with universal pension accounts, and repeal the individual alternative minimum tax. On the business side it would set a flat 35% corporate rate while eliminating many corporate tax breaks, impose stiff penalties on tax-shelter promoters, and claw back breaks for major integrated oil companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Working families with children would get a much larger standard deduction (about $15,000 for singles, more for couples) and a refundable credit of up to $2,500 per qualifying child that phases out above $60,000 of income ($120,000 for couples). Students and their families would get a refundable credit of up to $3,000 for tuition. Homeowners who don't itemize could deduct mortgage interest, savers could contribute up to $4,000-$5,000 a year to a new universal pension account regardless of income phase-outs, and millions of taxpayers would stop paying the alternative minimum tax. The bill's stated purpose includes partially offsetting the federal deficit with the new revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children and college students

how_it_helps.text: Increases the basic standard deduction to $15,000 for singles and 200% of that amount for joint filers, so far more households pay no tax on their first dollars of income without itemizing [S3].

Replaces the earned income credit and child tax credit with a simplified family credit of $2,500 per qualifying child (up to three), phasing out above $60,000 of income for singles and $120,000 for couples, with refunds exempt from being counted against housing and food assistance benefits [S3].
Creates a refundable credit of up to $3,000 for college tuition and fees, replacing the existing Hope and Lifetime Learning credits [S2] [S3].
Treats capital gains and dividends as ordinary income by repealing the 2003 rate reductions, ending a preference that mostly benefits higher-income investors [S2] [S3].
Repeals the individual alternative minimum tax, which increasingly caught middle-income households [S2] [S3].

Lets non-itemizers deduct home mortgage interest and lets all workers deduct contributions to new universal pension accounts of up to $4,000-$5,000 a year, while giving small employers a small credit for setting the accounts up [S2] [S3].

Raises revenue to partially offset the deficit by imposing a flat 35% corporate tax while terminating special exclusions, deductions, and credits, and by tightening penalties on abusive tax shelters [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income investors would pay more as capital gains and dividends are taxed at ordinary rates. Itemizers who rely on deductions the bill terminates would lose them, and families earning above the credit phase-outs would lose the child credit and dependent exemptions they currently claim. Major integrated oil companies would lose amortization of geological and geophysical costs and face inventory revaluation rules. Promoters of abusive tax shelters would face penalties of 100% of gross income derived from the activity, and government contractors would have 3% withheld from their payments. Alcohol and tobacco consumers would pay more as those excise taxes are adjusted for inflation.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-income investors, oil companies, shelter promoters

drawbacks.text: Families with modified adjusted gross income above $60,000 ($120,000 joint) would lose the $2,500-per-child credit entirely, and the bill repeals the child tax credit and dependent exemptions, so many middle-income households above the phase-out could pay more than they do today [S3].

The bill repeals a long list of deductions, exclusions, and preferences, which would raise taxes for households and businesses that currently use them, including workers receiving employer education assistance [S2] [S3].
The 3% withholding requirement on government payments for goods and services would create cash-flow and paperwork burdens for contractors, vendors, and state and local governments [S3].
The bill sunsets after 2010, so the entire rewritten system would expire within four years, creating planning uncertainty for families and businesses [S2] [S3].

The corporate side is a trade of a flat 35% rate for fewer loopholes, which would raise taxes for corporations that currently pay well below 35% while cutting nothing for those already at the top rate [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: bigger credits and a larger standard deduction for working families, paid for by taxing investment income like wages and stripping out preferences that mostly help high earners and big companies. But the family credit phases out sharply at $60,000 of income, so a wide band of middle-class parents would lose credits they now receive while continuing to pay 25% rates, and the loss of numerous deductions would hit households in high-cost states hardest. Without a formal revenue score in the record, the exact winners and losers by income cannot be verified, and the four-year sunset adds instability.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rahm Emanuel introduced the Fair Flat Tax Act of 2006 in the House on April 25, 2006 [S1] [S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation [S5].
No cosponsors signed on from either party [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 with the bill still sitting in committee [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The current tax code's beneficiaries kept everything: high-income investors retained lower capital gains and dividend rates, major oil companies kept their tax breaks, and tax-shelter promoters faced no new penalties. Middle-income families above the proposed credit phase-out also avoided potential tax increases the bill would have imposed on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Investors, oil companies, and shelter promoters

for.name: Rahm Emanuel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it as a complete rewrite of the individual and corporate income tax codes.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: The House committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 25, 2006 and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill while chairing the committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes occurred and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition beyond the Republican-led committee declining to act [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill eliminates amortization of geological and geophysical expenditures for integrated oil companies and requires revaluation of their LIFO crude oil and natural gas inventories, raising their taxable income [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Tax shelter promoters and tax advisory firms
industries.note: The bill sets a penalty of 100% of gross income for promoting abusive shelters or aiding understatement of tax liability, codifies the economic substance doctrine, and sharply raises criminal penalties for tax fraud [S2] [S3].
Repealing the 2003 capital gains and dividend rate cuts means investment income is taxed at ordinary rates up to 35%, a direct cost to households that earn most income from investments [S2] [S3].
A 3% withholding on government payments for goods and services ties up contractor cash flow and adds compliance costs, though it also improves tax collection from vendors who underreport [S3].

industries.industry: Retirement account and financial services providers
industries.note: The bill terminates new contributions to traditional and Roth IRAs but channels that tax-advantaged saving into new universal pension accounts administered by banks and trustees, preserving the industry's gatekeeper role [S3].

industries.industry: Distilled spirits, beer, wine, and tobacco producers
industries.note: Excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco would rise with inflation, cutting consumption or squeezing margins, with the higher cost largely passed on to consumers [S2] [S3].
